findings.title: Cutover arms destructive reconciliation before a watched reconcile
findings.description: When the arm file is absent, the weekly job skips its destructive offsite reconciliation and reports that it was unarmed. The cutover then creates the arm file anyway, enabling a later scheduled run to perform destructive sync and purge operations without the watched first reconcile required by the backup workflow. Preserve that safety gate instead of creating the arm file automatically here.

findings.title: Cluster roots can escape the `/data/` boundary
findings.description: The prefix check accepts paths such as `/data/../../etc/cron.d`: they begin with `/data/` but resolve outside it. `setup-backup.sh` uses these configured roots for directory ownership and mode changes as well as backup paths. Validate normalized path containment under `/data/`; the Python parser has the same prefix-only check.

findings.title: Health checks can pass using a stale log entry
findings.description: `run_health` ignores the return code from the health command and accepts the last `FLAGS` line in the log. If the command fails before writing a new entry, a previous clean entry can make the cutover report health as passing. Check the command result and verify that the parsed log entry was produced by this invocation.

findings.title: Backup network paths lack the required load-test coverage
findings.description: The added cutover tests replace the host calls, and there is no load-tier test exercising the new backup/offsite path with realistic resource or latency bounds. This path performs WAL pushes and remote verification, which can expose throughput and resource issues that the mocked unit tests cannot detect.
